concepts.title: Formulating a Linear Programming Problem
concepts.definition: Translate a resource-planning story into mathematics by naming the decision variables, writing the linear objective worth optimising, and listing every linear restriction including non-negativity of the variables.
concepts.formula: Z = a * x + b * y subject to linear constraints
concepts.key_idea: Objective function plus linear constraints plus non-negative variables.

concepts.title: Feasible Region of the Constraints
concepts.definition: Graphing every constraint as a half plane, their common area is the feasible region; its points are the feasible solutions, everything outside is infeasible, and the region is always convex, being bounded or unbounded.
concepts.formula: feasible region equals the overlap of all constraint half planes
concepts.key_idea: The feasible region is the shared area of all half planes including the axes.

solution_steps.explain: Turn each inequality into its boundary line.
Pick the side that satisfies the inequality, using a test point if needed.
The overlap of all half planes with x, y >= 0 is the feasible region.

concepts.title: Corner Point Method
concepts.definition: The optimum of a linear objective over a feasible region sits at a vertex, so list the corner points, evaluate the objective at each, and read off the largest or smallest value; for two corners tied at the optimum, the whole joining segment is optimal.
concepts.formula: the optimal value of Z occurs at a corner point of the feasible region
concepts.key_idea: Check Z only at the vertices; the best one answers the problem.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh206.txt corner point method steps with examples 1-3 (lines ~196-353)

concepts.title: Objective Value at a Corner Point
concepts.definition: The profit or cost standing of any candidate plan follows by substituting the plan's coordinates into the linear objective, which is exactly the per-corner arithmetic of the corner point method.
concepts.key_idea: Weight the coordinates by the objective coefficients and add.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh206.txt corner value tables with examples 1-2 (lines ~199-308)

concepts.title: Intersection of Two Boundary Lines
concepts.definition: A corner point of the feasible region is where two constraint boundary lines cross, so solving those two linear equations together supplies the vertex coordinates needed for the corner point method.
concepts.formula: vertex coordinates come from solving the two boundary equations
concepts.key_idea: Vertices are pair-wise crossings of the constraint lines.

concepts.title: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
concepts.definition: A bounded feasible region guarantees both a maximum and a minimum of the objective, each at a vertex; an unbounded region may deliver neither, and a candidate value counts only if the open half plane of strictly better values never meets the region.
concepts.formula: a bounded feasible region forces both an optimum maximum and minimum of Z
concepts.key_idea: Bounded means both extremes exist; unbounded needs the half plane check.

concepts.title: Multiple Optimal Solutions
concepts.definition: When two corner points deliver the same optimal value, every plan on the segment joining them matches it, so the problem has infinitely many optimal solutions along that edge.
concepts.formula: equal optimal values at two corners make the joining segment optimal
concepts.key_idea: A tie between vertices spreads the optimum along the connecting segment.

concepts.title: Infeasible Constraint Systems
concepts.definition: If the constraint half planes share no common point, the feasible region is empty, the problem admits no feasible solution, and no optimum can be reported.
concepts.formula: an empty overlap of constraint half planes means no feasible solution
concepts.key_idea: No common region means the problem has no answer to optimise.
